I'm also dropping links to [music] every single one of these in the description, so you don't have to hunt for anything. Let's get into number one, Superpowers. And it's the single most impactful thing that I've done for my Claude Code setup this year. Here's the problem that it solves. By default, when you ask Claude to do something, it just starts doing it. You type a prompt, it starts writing the code or making changes. No planning, no clarifying questions, no verification, which sounds efficient until you realized it misunderstood what you wanted and now you're spending tokens fixing something that should have been right the first time. Superpowers is a free plugin that installs 14 skills into Claude Code and forces it through a proper five-phase process on everything it does. Clarify, design, plan, code, verify. Before Claude writes a single line, it stops and asks the right question. It maps out the plan with the exact file path and task breakdowns. And at the end, it verifies what it built actually works. a proper test on this, 12 automated sessions, six with Superpowers, six without. Same prompts, same model. We got 9% cheaper runs, 14% fewer token used, and measurably better output quality on anything that wasn't trivially simple. One of my favorite parts of the plugin is the visual brainstorming companion. When you ask Claude to design something, Superpowers spins up a local web dashboard where it shows you options, mock-ups, and layouts before committing to anything. You pick what looks right, it builds from there. No more imagining what the results will look like, you see it first. However, where you don't want to use Superpowers is when you're doing fast iterative design. Say you want to change a button on your website, do not use Superpowers, it's just a huge waste of time. So, I personally use it when I start a big project or feature cuz it's just so good at asking questions. To install it, open Claude Code, type plugin in the chat, and hit enter. That opens up the Claude Code plugin marketplace. From there, grab the GitHub link from the description, paste it into the marketplace search, and add it. Once it's added, go to your plugin section, find Superpowers in the list, and just enable it. Done. And if you want to go deeper on this, check it out, link in the description. The second skill is the Notebook LM integration. And if you haven't seen this one yet, it's going to be the one that surprises you the most. Google's Notebook LM is one of the most powerful pre-research tools that has ever been built. You give it sources like PDFs, YouTube videos, web articles, and it generates slide decks, podcast-style audio summaries, mind maps from those sources. It's an incredible tool, but the way most people use it, manually adding sources one by one and clicking generate button button by button, is the slow version. When you connect it to Claude Code, you skip all of that. One prompt is all it takes. You say, "Hey Claude, research the latest trends in AI for creators, load 20 sources from YouTube and the web, and generate a notebook with a slide deck and a podcast overview." Claude does the entire job. It finds the sources, loads them into Notebook LM, and generates the assets without you opening Notebook LM once. The thing I want to make clear is that Notebook LM is completely free to use, which means that you can run unlimited research sessions, build unlimited notebooks, generate unlimited podcasts at zero cost. Thought handles the curation and automation, Notebook LM handles the heavy processing, and you just get the output delivered. To set this up, you need a skill file that connects Claude Code to Notebook LM. It installs a Python package under the hood that asks you to log in with your Google account once. After that, it just works. I have a full dedicated video on this setup step-by-step walk-through. It's in the description, and the skill file itself is completely free in the school community. Number three, Karpathy's Graphify. Okay, this one comes from Andrej Karpathy, one of the founding members at OpenAI, and one of the most respected names in AI. He talked publicly about how he uses knowledge graphs for his own projects on how to make AI navigation dramatically more efficient. Someone took that concept and built Graphify, a tool that applies the same approach to codebases and project files in Claude Code. Here's the problem it solves. Every time that you start a new Claude Code session, it has to reread your files and understand what's going on. In a small Claude project, that's fine, but if you got a project with hundreds of files, Claude spends a massive amount on tokens figuring out what connects to what before it even starts helping you. Graphify solves that by just turning your entire project into a queryable knowledge graph before the session starts. Think of it like this. Your project is a city, every file is a building, every import or connection is a road. Graphify maps all these roads out so Claude can navigate directly to what it needs instead of walking every street by foot. The result up to 70 times cheaper when you're querying a large codebase because Claude rides the graph directly to the relevant parts instead of loading everything [clears throat] from scratch. It works across 25 plus programming languages and it's multimodal. It can read PDFs and audio files, too. To use it, just install the repo, run Graphify command in your project, and then use a slash command to query it. The visual graphic generates is also genuinely useful on screen during filming. It shows which files are the Grand Central Stations of your project and which are the stops on the line. You get the best results on projects with 500 files or more. For smaller projects, uh the overhead just isn't worth it. But then, we got number four, Firecrawl. If you've ever tried to scrape a website or had Claude try to do it, you know the problem. The web is a mess. Cookie banners, infinite scroll, JavaScript that loads content after the page, ads everywhere. When AI reads a raw webpage, it ends up with a wall of HTML noise instead of the actual content, which means you burn tokens processing garbage, and the output is worse than it should be. Firecrawl is an AI agent tool that takes any URL and converts it into clean, structured data that AI can actually use. No HTML soup, no ad content, no banners, just uh meaningful information. And the token savings are real, up to 80% cheaper compared to feeding raw HTML into Claude because there's just less noise to process. The real use case I want to show you is lead generation because this is something creators and operators actually care about. Let me show you what happens when we give Claude a prompt like, "Use Firecrawl to find me the 20 leads in the pool cleaning business in Austin. I want their name, email, website, and two interesting facts from their site. Give me the results as an interactive HTML doc." Claude fires off the request, Firecrawl pulls the data from the web, and a few minutes later we got a fully formatted document with 20 real businesses, their contact details, and insights pulled from their websites. You can export it as a JSON, CSV, Excel, every format you need. And you can run the exact same approach for competitor research, content research, or any other intelligence gathering that you do manually right now. To set it up, go to Claude Code, manage connectors, and add a custom connector. Paste in your Firecrawl MCP server URL from their docs. You'll need an API key. Create a free account and you'll get 500 credits to start. The free tier is actually generous for getting started. But then, we got number five, Awesome Design. The last one is for anyone who's ever tried to build a website or landing page with Claude Code and got something that technically works, but looks like it was built in 2009. Claude Code is generally impressive at writing functional code, but design, it doesn't have a natural eye for what looks great unless you give it a reference. And that's the exact thing that Awesome Design does. It's a GitHub library with 68 complete design systems. Each one built by reverse-engineering a visual identity of some of the best-designed brands in the world. We're talking Apple, Lamborghini, Claude itself, and dozens more. Each design system has the typography, the color palette, the spacing rules, the component styles, everything. You tell Claude which one to use, and it builds your site in that aesthetic. No mood boards, no back and forth, no designer. Here's what this looks like in practice. I install the repo into Claude code and say, "Build me a landing page for my AI automation service in the style of Claude." Claude reads the Claude design system, the typography, the navy, the white palette, the clean minimal layout, and outputs a fully styled page that actually looks professional. And if I want to tweak it, I just say, "Change the headline, make the call to action button more permanent." Done in seconds. One thing to know is that this is a library, not a skill. So, these are predefined design templates, not indefinitely customizable from scratch. The quality does vary across the 68 options. So, my recommendation is to run it two or three times with the same prompt, and pick the best output. The top designs, the ones inspired by companies like Apple and Claude, are generally impressive. Start there. And that's all five. You can install every single one of these in a single conversation with Claude code. Links to all five are in the description. Go run them, and your agent is about to get a serious upgrade.

videos.title: OpenAI Just Open Sourced Their Agent Orchestrator. The Real Lesson Is The 3 Layers Underneath.
videos.description:
👉 Access our AI Architects course & join hundreds of serious AI builders in our community
https://www.theaiautomators.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=tutorial&utm_content=openai_symphony

Links:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJCe8hvZrxs
https://openai.com/index/open-source-codex-orchestration-symphony/
https://martinfowler.com/articles/harness-engineering.html
https://github.com/openai/symphony
https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/

OpenAI just open-sourced Symphony, their internal orchestration spec for scaling autonomous coding agents, and it highlights one of the biggest shifts happening in AI engineering right now. As coding agents become more capable, humans become the bottleneck, and the real work moves from writing code to building the scaffolding around the agents.

In this video, I break down the mental models behind agent harness engineering and show you how to think about building reliable autonomous systems at scale. Whether you're trying to scale Claude Code beyond a few chat sessions, or designing orchestration into your own AI powered apps, these frameworks will help you architect systems that actually work in production.

What's covered:
- The definition of an agent harness and why the term has become so broad
- The inner harness vs outer harness mental model from Brigetta Berkeler's harness engineering article
- How the AI model acts like a CPU while the harness manages memory, sub agents, tool execution, and more
- Why metaprompting frameworks like Superpowers, GSD, and BMAD only get you so far
- Guides vs sensors: steering agents forward and feeding deterministic and inferential checks back in
- Why computational sensors like linters, types, and schemas are heavily underused by AI builders
- LLM as a judge and inferential sensor patterns for feedback loops
- Ralph Wiggum loops as a simple example
- Extending the mental model to harness layers in AI apps that you build
- The deterministic vs probabilistic spectrum for harnesses
- The orchestrator and scheduler layer sitting above inner and outer harnesses

How OpenAI's Symphony spec uses Linear as the human interface for ticket-based agent work
Solving the two biggest problems with parallel agents: clashing and human in the loop design

The future of AI engineering is less about prompting and more about scaffolding. The model is the CPU, but the harness is where the real engineering happens.

If you want to go deeper on AI architecture, harness engineering, and agentic retrieval, check out our AI Architects course linked above.

Chapters:
0:00 - Overview
0:47 - OpenAI Symphony spec
2:35 - What is an agent harness
4:20 - Inner vs outer harness
5:24 - Guides and sensors
7:34 - Harness layers in AI apps
8:37 - The orchestrator layer
9:46 - Getting started with Symphony

videos.transcript_text: OpenAI just published a fascinating article about their new open-source agent orchestrator to help overcome the biggest bottlenecks they encountered when trying to scale autonomous coding agents. And there are some interesting insights here that could really help us all when we're building our own agentic systems. Back in February, OpenAI showed a relatively controversial experiment they were running internally to create software with zero lines of manually written code. Instead of micromanaging the coding agents, the primary job of the engineer was now to create scaffolding around the coding agent to enable it to do work with less supervision. As these systems became increasingly efficient, humans could no longer keep up with coding agents and all of a sudden the humans were now the biggest bottleneck in the process. And that was the birth of OpenAI's open-sourced Symphony orchestration spec. So what exactly is Symfony? Well, at its core, Symfony is an agent orchestrator that takes an issue tracker like Linear here and turns it into a tool that can trigger coding agents. The concept here is pretty simple. For every ticket on this board, Symphfony makes sure there's a coding agent running for it in its own isolated workspace, working continuously until the ticket is done. And OpenAI are essentially creating a state machine flow using linear here. This can then potentially allow teams to work at a higher level of abstraction rather than just babysitting and supervising individual coding sessions. And in theory, less technical staff members can also get involved in the process. When you go to the GitHub repo, the first thing you'll notice is that this is mostly just a spec.md file, but they also have a prototype version you can use created in Elixir, which I'll talk about in a few minutes. OpenAI encourage you to point your favorite coding agent at the spec and then have it implement its own version in whatever language you want and also get it to orchestrate against whatever coding agent you want, not just codecs. So you don't have to have a codec subscription to run this. Surprisingly enough, even the OpenAI article shows some post on X where people are showing how they implemented this to orchestrate cloud code sessions. So you have two options to run with here. If you want to use their reference elixir implementation, you can clone the repo and then get your coding agent to help with the setup. Then you can connect that to a linear account using your personal API key and then that will continuously pull the tickets here. That then calls Codeex in app server mode and app server mode runs the codeex CLI as a longived process and then Symfony can then call that programmatically. There's certainly plenty of OpenAI marketing within this article. Like they've stated that this has resulted in a 500% increase in landed pull requests on some teams, but countless devs have converged on similar types of systems to this. And OpenAI are certainly not the first dev team to build orchestration around coding agents. I think the most important lesson here is unpacking the architectural layers that make a system like this work and how we can then make effective use of those systems in our own projects. And many of you watching this will already know that attempting to scale AI coding agents beyond a few concurrent chat sessions definitely comes with its own set of challenges. So you may be staring at a coding chat window wondering how do I turn this into a reliable autonomous agent at scale for my project. Or you may want to build advanced orchestration features into your AI powered apps but you're getting lost in the architecture. I'm going to share some great mental models and resources that I find really useful. Let's start by clearing up some ambiguity about the term agent harness, which at this point could mean many different things. As Philip Schmid put it, "An agent harness is the infrastructure that wraps around an AI model." As you can see from his clearly AI generated image here, the agent harness manages the vast majority of the work within our AI systems. And he compares the AI model to that of the CPU of a computer in that it is very important, but it has a very specific function. An LLM is really only able to reason about its responses and then generate an output such as text. Everything beyond that from the illusion of memory and chat history to managing sub agents to actually managing the execution of tool calls that's all actually managed within the harness code. So the definition of an agent harness is incredibly broad. And to make better sense of this we're going to borrow some mental models from Vetta Berkeler's great article on harness engineering where she suggested that we should view agent harnesses in two separate layers. The first is the inner harness. The inner harness is everything that ships inside your AI coding agent, whether it be cloud code or cursor or codecs. Of course, they're very powerful out of the box already. They ship inside with the ability to manage sub agents, sandbox code execution, skills, hooks, tools, permissions, and more. But as Brigitta writes in this article, to let coding agents work with less supervision, we need ways to increase our confidence in their result. But how exactly do we do that? As a starting point, we can try and give our coding agents better context of the overall code base. We can try and convince them to do a better job via better prompting. And we can also use meta prompting frameworks such as superpowers or GSD version one or VMAD. And those things absolutely help, but they only go so far. And that's where the real engineering of the outer harness comes into play. Coding agents such as Claude or Codeex expose features that let us build an outer harness around them. And these harnesses are actual code that controls the agent life cycle programmatically. So instead of using a meta prompting framework where we might ask the AI agent to reset the context, the outer harness can actually deterministically terminate the session, clear the context, read the task state from disk, inject the relevant files, and then work from there. So Ralph loops or projects like Gas Town or Archon are all examples of systems that act as outer harnesses. In this article, it said that the harness acts like a cybernetic governor combining feed forward and feedback to regulate the codebase towards the desired state. That feedback mechanism is one of the most important parts of this process. There's a very useful distinction between guides and sensors here where the guides help steer the agent in the right direction. So these are anything that tries to make the agents first attempt better. So your agent might read from an agent's MD file or you may provide skills and playbooks and examples that they can work from. But the AI agent is not always going to get things right and even if so not necessarily according to your own behaviors and rules and that's where the very important feedback loop comes in and these are referred to as sensors. So we might have deterministic computationalbased sensors such as llinters and types and schemas. So for example whenever your coding agent creates code you can run those through deterministic checks without using AI at all and then feed that back to the model. And one of the main arguments made within this article is that these computational type checks are heavily underused by AI builders. Of course, you can also have sensors powered by AI known as inferential sensors such as you can feed code generated by an LLM into another call to an LLM, ideally another model where it can act as a judge and then that can be fed back into the model and humans then continuously steer and optimize the components of this outer harness. If we go back to our OpenAI article on harness engineering, they've run with this type of concept where the agent is called in a Ralph Wigum loop until all human reviewers are satisfied. Running an external Ralph Wigum loop, not the one built into Claude code directly, by the way, is a very simple example of an outer harness. It can just keep spawning Claude sessions again and again and again through brute force iteration until a certain goal has been met. and other outer harnesses can just take this thin orchestrator concept as a starting point and bring it many steps further and potentially in many different directions. Archon is a great example of a tool that allows you to create your own outer harnesses which can enforce your agents to act in a certain deterministic way. It already includes a lot of out ofthe-box workflows and it even allows for parallel executions of tasks. We use this inner outer harness distinction as a mental model not only for coding agents but also for agentic systems we build. In our full stack AI builder series, Daniel walks through the creation of a contract review harness that adds deterministic aspects to the agentic workflow. And this can essentially be seen as an outer harness, a configurable aspect that's layered on top of the inner harness core functionality of the agentic system. It can have guides and sensors that are automatically fed back into the agent such as automated computational document checks that don't use AI at all as well as inferential checks such as LLM as a judge. And these harnesses will lie on a spectrum between either being very deterministic or very probabilistic. That contract review harness tends to follow a very specific workflow. But many other harnesses will be a lot more open-ended, such as deep research harnesses. And these are essentially the opposite shape. They're broad, open-ended, and agentic throughout, but they can still have plenty of deterministic scaffolding around them, such as computational checking of citations or multiple layers of LM reviews before they're passed back for human review. As we start building upon the scaffolding on top of our AI agents, you may even consider that they start becoming their own layer on top of the mental model we've talked about already. And this layer could be seen as the overarching orchestrator or scheduler layer. And that's very much where OpenAI positions systems created using their new symphony spec as this is really multi-agent orchestration at a higher level. These are all mental models and metaphors. They just help our general understanding of the concepts and the lines can very much be blurred between them. For example, Gas Town is an orchestration framework where it takes the concept of a Ralph Wiggum loop have many of them running at once along with automated orchestration around those instances. And this can certainly get quite chaotic. But frameworks like this are trying to solve the problem of getting many agents to work reliably in parallel. And the two biggest issues that people face other than their intense token usage and AI builds with systems like this is twofold. It's making AI agents work reliably together without clashing and adding in the correct human in the loop layers where humans are in the most important parts of the process without micromanaging everything because that becomes the biggest bottleneck and again that's where we come back to this Symfony spec. Symfony started with a concept that any open task should get picked up and completed by an agent instead of developers managing codec sessions in multiple tabs. They made this issue tracker in linear and use that as the human interface. Those tickets then trigger the coding agent to work autonomously on those tasks as required and then report back to the user when required. If you want to get started with the Symfony open-source spec, it's available on the GitHub repo linked below. And you can get your own coding agent to create an orchestration system based on this spec in whatever language you want, or you can also use their out-of-the-box demo example. In this video, we went through a lot of AI architecture concepts. If you found that useful, you should definitely check out our AI architects course linked below, which will help give you a deeper understanding of AI systems, technical foundations, harness engineering, agentic retrieval, and more. And if you like this video, you'll love the previous video on our channel where Daniel goes through a deep dive into the various agent frameworks and services you can use when building out AI systems.

바람 세기는 다이슨이 앞승이었습니다. 요것도 두 제품의 특징이랄까요? 사실 루베 같은 경우는 일반적으로 나와 있는 손손기의 특징이랑 거의 비슷해요. 뒤에서 공기를 흡입해서 이렇게 쫙 넓게 퍼트려 주려는 느낌이 있고 다이슨 같은 경우에는이 허시젯라는 그 용어를 썼잖아요. 얘는 바람이 퍼지지 않고 직진성이 되게 강하면서 매끄러운 바람을 만들어 주더라고요. 그게 마치 강하게 압축된 공기를 직진으로 빵 쏴 주는 느낌이랄까요? 그런 걸 보면 다이슨이 가격이 비싸고 좀 요상하게 생기긴 했지만 허치시대 기술이 단순히 마케팅은 아닌가 봐요. 대신 커버되는 바람에 면적은 루메나가 더 좋았습니다. 마치 그거를 생각하면 돼요. 루메나 같은 경우에는 일반적인 선풍기의 느낌, 바이슨 같은 경우에는 서큘레이터의 느낌이랄까요? 근데 또 실제로 체감했을 때 오랫동안 써 보니까 그런 차이 있었었습니다. 가까운 거리에서는 다이슨이 바람에 센 거는 맞지만 면적이 그렇게 넓진 않단 말이에요. 그래서 장기적으로 봤을 때는 루메나가 체감상 더 시원한 느낌이 들었습니다. 근데 또 그런 건 있어요. 저도 실내에서 테스트했을 때 그리고 지금은 밖에 그렇게 많이 덥진 않단 말이에요. 만약에 엄청 뜨거운 여름이라고 생각한다면 이도 저도 아닌 것보다 다이슨 쪽이 더 시원할 수 있을 것 같기도 하더라고요. 그리고 손선폭이 쓰다 보면 또 이제 우리가 느끼는게 뭐냐면 생각보다 이게 진동이 좀 있습니다. 진동은 다 있음이 앞승이에요. 왜냐면 루메라는 잔진동이 있는 느낌이랄까요. 자 봐요. 얘 같은 경우에 바닥에 뒀을 때 진동으로 인해서 소음이 좀 생기고 다이스는 풀파워로 해도 바닥에 진동이 느껴지지 않습니다.이 진동은 그냥 다이슨 앞승이에요. 그럼 다음으로 넘어가서 이제 소음이랑 바르은 어땠느냐? 요거는 루메나가 훨씬 더 좋았다. 왜냐면 다이스는 1단부터 바람은 세지만 얘는 시끄러워서 1단으로도 실내에서 쓰기에는 좀 무리였습니다. 봐요. 일단 또 실내서는 꽤 시끄러워요. 바람이 센 대신. 일단 일단 당연히 바람 세기에 차이가 있긴 하지만 나는 바람 세기는 되게 약하고 되게 조용하게 쓰고 싶어 하시는 분들에게는 루베너가 더 좋을 거예요. 그리고 이제 바르 같은 경우에는 제가 이제 배터리 테스트를 하면서도 여러 가지로 봤지만 완을 때 바르이 좀 심하다. 그런 느낌은 전혀 없었습니다. 배터리 같은 경우 스펙상 최대 6여시간 사용 가능하다고 합니다. 그리고 충전 시간은 3세시간 있고요. 루베네랑 다이슨을 비교한다. 배터리는 루메나가 앞승이었습니다. 둘 다 최대 풍속으로 테스트했을 땐 루메나는 2시간 34분 10초가 같고요. 다이스는 49분 58초가 같습니다. 그러니까 최고 세기에서 루메나가 1시간 44분 12초 더 오래 간 거예요. 배터리도 보면 루메나가 4,800m어. 다이슨 5,000m어. 물리적으로 다이슨의 배터리가 더 크죠. 그렇기 때문에 배터리만 봤을 때는 루메가 더 좋다. 물론 여러 가지로 고려한다면 다이슨의 풍속이 그만큼 더 세기 때문에 더 짧다고 할 수도 있기도 하지만 풀로 충전했을 때 풀 세기로 한시간도 못 간다. 아쉽긴 하죠. 그리고 충전 속도 루메나가 더 좋았습니다. 루메나 같은 경우에는 14W 정도 먹는 것에 비해 다이스는 8W 정도로 충전 속도 차이가 꽤 나더라고요. 그렇다 보니 충전 시간도 많이 차이가 났습니다. 로메나 같은 경우에는 충전 속도는 1시간 49분이 걸렸고 바이스는 2시간 19분이 걸렸습니다. 그럼 방전 테스트도 진행해 봤을 땐 5단에선 약 50분, 4단에서선 1시간 19분, 3단에서 1시간 59분, 2단에서 2시간 40분, 1단에선 6시간 17분으로 세기에 따라 편차가 꽤 많이 있었습니다. 야, 다이스는 진짜 극과 극이에요.이 이 파워에 따라서 배터리가 엄청 많이 다른 느낌이랄까요? 그리고 배터리 자량 보는 것부터 되게 특이했어요. 얘는 실시간으로 보여지는게 아니라 전원을 끄고 나서 여기서 이제 플러스 버튼을 누르잖아요. 이렇게 다섯 개 LED 게이지로 배터리 잔량이 나오더라고요. 전원을 켠 상태에서는 여기서 나오지 않고요. 또 쓰다 보면 얘가 또 재밌는게 뭐냐면 여기 뒤에 또 LED가 있었습니다. 얘도 배터리 잔량이 20% 아래면 계속 이제 불이 들어와 있는 그러한 방식으로 배터리 잔량을 알려 준다. 요거 로메나처럼 숫자로 보여 주면 좋긴 하지만 뭐 요거 정도만 해도 괜찮은 느낌. 기타 사용기를 이야기해 보자면 먼저 얘는 이제 날개 없는 디자인입니다. 그래서 딱히 여기에 먼지가 낄 것 같진 않아요. 머리카락이 끼냐 걱정하실 분들도 있을 것 같은데 이게 구조상 바람을 밀어내는 형태라서 머리가 끼진 않습니다. 오히려 얘는 이제 펜이 있기 때문에 여기 중간에 펜 사이에 머리카락이 끼일 수 있지만요. 그리고 얘도 세척이 또 중요하잖아요. 그래서 사용자 설명서를 받습니다. 브러시로 털어서 사용하기를 권장하고 있더라고요. 요 이제 요런 손풍기들은 가방에서 버튼이 눌러서 켜져 있다가 배터리가 방전되는 케이스가 있거든요. 근데 얘는요 이제 버튼을 눌러서 켜는게 아니라 온오프 스위치로 있어서 제가 실제로 가방에 놓고 돌아냐 봐도 얘가 쉽게 켜지진 않았습니다. 그리고 또 이제 방수가 되냐 요것도 물어봐 주셨는데 IPX 등급이 표기가 없는 걸로 봐서는 방수는 될 거 같지 않다. 그리고 휴대성도 제가 실제로 들고 다녀 보니까 우회로 가이슨이 좋았습니다. 왜냐면 요런 형태의 손풍이 같은 경우에는 이제 손잡이는 작긴 한데 이제 위에가 좀 크기 때문에 약간의 부피감이 있는 것에 위에 얘는 이제 그냥 일직선으로 이렇게 이제 동그랗게 되어 있다 보니까 부피가 작아서 수납하기도 좋고 보관하기도 좋았습니다. 그리고 또 의외로 좋은 점이 제가 책상에서 테스트를 좀 했거든요. 요런 일반적인 손풍기는 이제 앞으로 바람이 쏴 주기 때문에 요렇게 테이블 위에 두게 된다면 이게 제 얼굴에 바로 오지 않아요. 근데 바이스는 그냥 테이블 위에 두잖아요. 얘가 살짝 각도가 있다 보니까 얼굴로 직방으로 와요. 이것도 생각보다 좋았습니다. 그리고 필요할 때는 얘가 이제 좀 제한적이긴 하지만 360도로 돌려서 위쪽으로도 바람을 보낼 수 있다. 근데 이거는 거의 잘 안 쓰게 돼요. 아마 이제 목으로 걸어서 이렇게 쓰시는 분들은 좀 유용하게 쓸 수 있겠죠. 아, 그리고 무게. 무게도 생각보다 다이슨이 좋았습니다. 아무래도 얘는 이제 펠티어 소자가 들어가서 그런지 이제 무게감이 좀 있는 편이고 바이스는 크기 대비 그 부피 대비 좀 가벼운 느낌. 자, 요렇게 많은 분들께서 궁금해하실 다이슨에서 선풍기를 내놨다 해서 구입해 본 아이템 얘를 한번 살펴봤습니다. 가격 빼고 나면 나름 괜찮은 거 같기도 해요. 물론 아직까지 지금 막 무더운 여름이 아니라서 밖에서 써 보지 못했지만 생각보단 제품이 꽤 괜찮습니다. 15만 원으로 나오면은 좀 그거는 이제 곤란할 것 같고 한 10만 원 아랫대로 할인해서 구입할 수 있다. 의외로 그래도 꽤 수요가 있지 않을까 싶습니다. 실제로 진짜 엄청 무서운 여름에 제대로 한번 테스트 해 보고 싶은데요. 대신 실내에서 쓰기에는 소음이심해서 쓰긴 어렵다. 아무튼 오늘 여기까지며 곧 더워질 무더운 여름 아마 손풍기를 많이 구입하실 것 같은데 얘는 이제 가격이 비싸서 많이 구입할 것 같진 않지만 좀 재미 용도로 한번 살펴봤는데 생각보다 괜찮은 제품이었고 저희도 이번에 다이스를 테스트하면서요 폭력 테스트 제품을 사서 만약 기회가 된다면 많은 분들께서 궁금해한 제품을 댓글로 남겨 주시면 저희가 한번 손풍기들을 한번 모아서 리뷰를 해 보도록 하겠습니다. 아마 이제 곧 여름 시작이라서 많은 제조사에서 신제품을 출시할 것 같거든요.

중간 구간에서 툴, 사례, 비교 포인트를 빠르게 제시해 정보 밀도를 높인다.

큰 담론보다 작은 병목 하나를 해결해주는 포장 방식이 클릭으로 이어지기 쉽다.
transcript_highlights: 근데 다이슨이 진짜 되게 신기한 거는 여러 제품들을 되게 많이 만들어요. 그래서 이번에도 진짜 상상치도 못한 선풍기를 만들었고 위로 패키지는 조금 허접하긴 합니다. 여기까지 봤을 때는 알리에서 구입한 제품을 뜨는 느낌이랄까요?
그래서 요걸로도 한번 비교를 해 봤거든요. 일반적으로 손풍기를 많이 쓰는 15cm 거래에서 테스트를 해 봤을 땐 루메는 최대 풍속일 때 약 8.3m/s 다이스는 약 13.3m/s로 3m/세로 다이슨이 약 60% 정도 더 강했습니다.
그럼 이미 더운 야외 상태에서는 거의 찍가면 안 돼요. 그럼 요렇게 이제 단순히 바람 세기를 비교했을 때 어떤게 더 좋았을까? 바람 세기는 다이슨이 앞승이었습니다.

videos.title: Leisure's Not a Luxury. It's a Requirement for Top Leaders
videos.description:
For strivers, leisure may be the hardest skill to master--but it's also one of the most important. Arthur C. Brooks, author of "The Happiness Files" and "The Meaning of Your Life", argues that leisure is not laziness or escape, but a serious practice that can make us more creative, grounded, and effective. He challenges leaders to rethink “work-life balance” and instead pursue a more integrated, meaningful life. For ambitious professionals, the lesson is clear: learning how to use leisure well may be one of the most important skills for long-term happiness and success.

More from Arthur C. Brooks: http://themeaningofyourlife.com/ and https://www.amazon.com/Happiness-Files-Insights-Arthur-Brooks/dp/B0F4MFQ6VN

videos.transcript_text:
ARTHUR C. BROOKS: I'm
a classic striver. I work really hard. I want to put points on
the board every single day. You know what I'm bad at? Leisure. Now, I know what
you're thinking. Leisure is chilling
on the beach. And you're probably not very
good at leisure, either, if you're watching this video. You're watching content from HBR
because you want an edge, man. I completely get it. But here's where we're
wrong, fellow strivers. Leisure is a serious business. [JAZZ MUSIC] A very famous book written in
the middle of the 20th century called Leisure, the Basis
of Culture, by Josef Pieper, German philosopher-- he
was a great philosopher. And he said that we need
to be great at leisure. By that, he meant that we need
to be strivers at leisure, too. And that meant not being lazy. He talked about leisure
as being a serious thing in which we're not
compensated by the world, but which enriches us
and makes us better. You don't need
work-life balance. You need work-life integration. And the way to do that,
to be better at your job, is also to be better
at your "not job." The three parts of leisure
that make you truly excellent are all about learning things
you don't have to learn, deepening your relationships
for which nobody pays you, which is to say, not on the
clock, and becoming spiritually or philosophically
deeper than you once were. Those are the three
areas of leisure that you can dedicate
yourself to to get better at and watch your happiness
and your effectiveness and your productivity and
your creativity truly grow. And those are great
goals for any striver. I know you plan out your work. Every striver does. Every minute is
accounted for, right? And the trouble is that they
don't like the time when they're not working precisely
because it's so unstructured, feels like it's frittered away. I talk to people all the
time who say, boy, at work, I'm unbelievably productive. But then I come home,
and I'm exhausted. And I just waste
all my time-- zoom, zoom, zoom-- scrolling
through social media. And I feel bad about myself. The answer to that is to take
seriously your leisure time like you take your work. That means real
assignments and real goals, like having
objectives that you're trying to focus on to
be better than you once were so that you're looking
forward to get home not to do more work and not to fritter
away your time on social media, but to read that book that
you've always wanted to read. I promise you that if you set
aside The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoyevsky--
you probably always wanted to read it. Everybody did. It's so great. It's a complete page-turner. And you say, as soon as
I get home from work, I'm going to dig into that book. That's something that has the
dignity of every striver's work calendar. And you can dedicate
it to your leisure. And you can love both. You can go too far and suck
all the joy out of this if you say to
yourself, I'm not going to sleep until I've read 35
pages of The Brothers Karamazov by Dostoyevsky, then pretty
soon, you won't look forward to it anymore. It has to be something that
doesn't become a chore, it doesn't become
something that's a task that sucks the
meaning out of life, per se. One of the ways that
you can test this is to see whether or not
you're truly getting enjoyment from something. And if you are,
then you're going to want to be more
structured about it. You're going to want to
do it in a serious way. You're going to want
to get after it. You're going to
want to schedule it. But if it actually
becomes something that you're not
enjoying anymore, then you know that you've
actually gone too far. That's how you figure
it out, not too hard. Can leisure be unproductive? The answer, according
to Josef Pieper, who wrote Leisure,
the Basis of Culture, is no because if
you're doing something that's inherently generative
and good, that's productive. That doesn't mean
it's work itself. You don't have to turn
your leisure into a job. But it has to be something
where you have personal growth. Maybe that's total and
complete relaxation. Maybe that's going on
a retreat, where you're sitting in meditation
or in prayer, or you're getting serious about
deepening your relationship outside of the confines of any
of your work responsibilities. But that's productive. It's just a new way of seeing
what productivity actually is.

MATLAB Copilot이 단순한 코드 생성 도구를 넘어 어떻게 엔지니어링 작업 전반을 돕는지 살펴봤습니다.
기존 MATLAB이 가진 강력한 연구개발 라이브러리 및 프레임워크를 그대로 활용하면서도 반도체 웨이퍼 불량 데이터를 시각화하고, 결함 패턴과 수율을 빠르게 분석해보며 MATLAB Copilot으로 테스트해보았는데요.
특히 Simulink를 활용해 자율주행차의 긴급 제동 시스템 AEB 로직을 자연어로 구현할 때 AI를 활용해서 원하는 연구개발 모델을 테스트하고 검증하는 것, 복잡한 제어 로직도 MATLAB 환경 안에서 얼마나 직관적으로 만들 수 있는지 확인이 됩니다.
또한 Copilot이 코드 주석 생성이나 인라인 프롬프팅도 지원하는데요.
최근에는 MATLAB MCP를 통해 외부 AI 에이전트가 MATLAB을 직접 호출하고 실행할 수 있어서 Claude에 연결하여 사용도 해보았습니다.
MATLAB Copilot이 연구, 개발, 검증 업무를 어떻게 더 빠르고 유연하게 바꿀 수 있는지 보면서 엔지니어링 툴에 AI가 통합될 때 실제 현장에서 어떤 변화가 생기는지도 함께 짚어봤습니다.

AI 어시스턴트가 나왔습니다. 바로 코파일럿이라고 하는 건데요.이 매틀렛 코파일럿을 이용해 가지고 현재 업계 안에서 어떤 작업들을 하고 있는지 얼마나 빨리 가볍게 구현이 될 수 있는지를 한번 살펴보면서 몇 번 만에 한번 꺼내 보는 시현 해 보도록 하겠습니다. 요즘 채트T 같은 LM에도 코드 생성을 맡기는 분들이 많으신데 기본적으로 매틀렛 코파일럿이 그냥 videos.description:
최근 미국에서 NASA, MIT, Los Alamos, 항공우주, 핵융합, 국가안보 시설과 연결된 인물들의 사망·실종 사례가 하나의 사건처럼 묶이며 큰 논란이 되고 있습니다.

온라인에서는 이를 두고 “과학자 11명 실종 미스터리”라고 부르며 UFO, 비밀 프로젝트, 외국 정보기관 개입설까지 다양한 이야기가 확산되고 있습니다.

하지만 실제로 확인된 사실과 온라인에서 덧붙은 추정은 분리해서 볼 필요가 있습니다.

이번 영상에서는 주요 인물들의 실제 소속, 사건 정황, 확인된 수사 내용, 그리고 과장된 주장들을 하나씩 정리했습니다.

특히 NASA JPL, 로켓 엔진용 초합금, MIT 핵융합 연구, Los Alamos, Kansas City National Security Campus 같은 키워드가 왜 이 사건을 더 민감하게 만들었는지 살펴봤습니다.

현재까지 이 사건들이 하나의 조직적 암살이나 외국 정보기관 작전으로 연결됐다는 공개 증거는 없습니다.

그럼에도 미국 의회와 FBI가 왜 공통점 여부를 확인하려 하는지, 첨단기술 시대의 인적 보안 관점에서 짚어봤습니다.

핵심은 UFO 괴담이 아니라, 핵·우주항공·AI 인프라 시대에 사람과 연구기관, 계약자, 공급망이 모두 보안 표면이 되는 현실입니다.

이번 논란을 통해 첨단기술 경쟁에서 “사람”이 왜 중요한 기술 자산이 되는지 함께 살펴봅니다.

이런 거를 결국 사람이 결정을 해야 될 텐데 그런 부분에 있어서 많은 것들의 영역을 특히나 비핵 부품과 관련된 요런 부분들조차도 얘네를 완성해 나가는 그 과정에 대한 것들을 그냥 이게 레퍼런스 가이드로서 할 수가 있느냐 그런 관점에서 봤을 때 사람이 훨씬 더 중요한 것이 아니냐. 특히나 행무기는 굉장히 오랫동안 복원을 해야 되니까. 사실 이런 것들이 AI 경쟁 같은 것들이 물리인프라 경쟁을 지금 이동 중이잖아요. 그런 것점에서 보면은이 기술 패권이라고 하는 것도 결국은 사람 싸움이에요. 이런 거대한 GPU 데이터 센터 전력도 필요하고 냉각도 필요하고 반도체 공망도 필요하고 온갖게 다 필요하잖아요. 그러니까 행융합 전력도 구매하고 오픈에는 헬리온이랑 전략 파트너심 논의하고 SMR 원전 태양광도 넣고 온갖 것들 다 하고 있는데 이런 것들을 연결해서 보았을 때 자연스럽게 에너지랑 우주 인프라로 관심을 가지면서 가게 되는데 막 서로 막 그 인력들을 서로 뺏으려고 노력하고 있잖아요. 근데 이런 인프라들은 어떻게 투자해하고 계속 지울 수 있더라 하더라도 그거를 어떻게 만들 것이며 특정한 인력들이 어떻게 기억할 수 있는 그런 부분들은 사람이 백업이 불과한데 만약에 이런 인력들이 이탈이 된다면 어떻게 될 것이냐 이런 문제들이 발생하겠죠. 우리나라 같은 경우에도 지금은 메모리가 돈을 엄청나게 많이 벌고 있죠. 반도체에서 중심을 됐고 앞으로도 구조적으로 굉장히 많이 발전이 될 거라고 저도 기대하고 있고 굉장히 기원을 하고 있는데 정부에서 단체로 반도체 인력을 늘린다 이런 얘기를 막 하고 있음에도 불구하고 모자르하잖아요. 지금 인력 자체가 하이닉스는 성가금을 13억 받는데 삼성전자는 이제 그 상한이 정해져 있어서 2천만 원 밖에 못 받는다. 뭐 그런 얘기 나와서 그 삼성 직원들이 뭐 그런 얘기를 한다고 하잖아요. 인력 유출이 된다. 그래서 어떤 기자분이 이렇게 얘기를 하시더라고요. 그렇게 인력 빠지는 분들은 필요 없는 분이라고 정말 똑똑하신 분들은 그런 얘기 안 한다고 그러는데 제가 알고 있는 굉장히 많은 삼성분들은 전혀 그렇게 생각 안 하고요. 지금 사람이 모자아요. 지금 결국 인력들이 중심이 돼야 되는데 그 인력들이 여기에 있을 만한 이유가 없으면은 결국은 나가겠죠. 사실 그런 것들을 지금부터 구조적으로 시스템적으로 만들어 가야 된다고 생각이 들고 결국은 이거를 그냥 뭐 여러 가지 이렇게 웨이퍼의 패턴들이 있으면은 이게 뭐가 패턴이 아니냐라고 볼 수도 있고 그냥 뭐 바퀴 떨어졌네 이렇게 볼 수도 있고 독이 나름예요. 사실 음모론이란 것들이 다 그런 내용들이 있죠. 이거를 잘 엮으면은 패턴처럼 보이지만 그렇지 않은 경우는 사실 무작이로 또 보이거든요. 그래서 개별 사건들이 점검은 필요한 건 맞는데 이걸 직접적으로 해 가지고 뭔가 이렇게 음모론 해서 드려 보기보다는이 기술 트렌드를 계속 따라가는 입장에서 보면은 야 진짜 이거 인력이 없어지면은 이거 커버가 안 되는 세상이 될 수 있겠구나라는 생각이 들어왔고 그런 점에서 한번 이번 것들을 빠르게 리뷰를 해 보았고요. 여러 가지 은페서 사실 온라인에서 바열을 되고 있는 거는요 정도밖에이 가능성이 낮지만도 이게 제일 많이 바를 되고 있고 대부분 통계적 착시라고 볼 수가 있습니다. 결국 제가 이슈를 바라보면서 드리고 싶었던 말씀은 결국 연구자가이 실패했던 경험이라든가 성공했던이 모든 엔지니어링의 공정 노하우 이런 것들 있잖아요. 혹은이 공급망 지식이라든가 이런 것들도 행정 인력의 어떤 조직 네트워크조차도 넓은 의미로 보면 어떤 보안의 영역으로 올 수가 있다라는 거죠. 지금 같이 전 세계가 블록화가 되고 있고 서로 프리 트레이딩이 안 되고 있는 상황에서는이 안묵지 때문에 누군가가 표적이 됐다라고 하기보다는 안묵지가 굉장히 중요한 요소가 되기 때문에이 사람의 실종과 사망조차도 단순 개인 사건인지 아니면 기술 안보 리스크인지를 구분하기 힘든 시점에 온게 아닌가 약간 요런 회색 지대가 느껴져 가지고 오늘 한번 영상을 만들게 되었습니다. 지금까지 에로였습니다.

2. 피그마 커뮤니티의 검증된 UI 키트를 클로드 디자인에 업로드하여 일관된 퀄리티를 확보할 수 있다.
3. 클로드 디자인은 주니어 디자이너 수준의 보조 화면을 순식간에 제작하며 업무 시간을 획기적으로 단축한다.

📝 세부 내용 요약 (Section Summaries)
■ 클로드 디자인의 등장과 디자인 생태계의 변화
클로드 디자인은 현직 디자이너들이 의존하던 피그마의 영역을 공략하며 시장에 큰 충격을 주고 있습니다. 실제로 클로드 디자인을 만든 제작자가 피그마 출신이라는 점이 흥미로우며, 이제는 코딩과 디자인, 커뮤니케이션의 경계가 허물어지는 새로운 작업 방식이 정착되고 있습니다.

■ 디자인 시스템: 고품질 결과물의 핵심 기초
고품질의 일관된 디자인을 얻기 위해서는 사전 세팅인 디자인 시스템이 필수입니다. 애플의 iOS나 구글의 머티리얼 디자인 시스템, 혹은 한국의 원티드 디자인 시스템 같은 .fig 파일을 클로드 디자인에 업로드하고 AI가 이를 학습하게 함으로써 전문적인 결과물을 도출할 수 있습니다.

■ PRD 기반의 실무 워크플로우와 프로토타이핑
단순한 명령어가 아닌 PRD(제품 요구사항 문서)를 먼저 작성하여 AI에게 문맥을 제공하는 것이 중요합니다. 시니어 택시 앱 사례처럼 구체적인 기획서를 기반으로 가설을 설정하고, 이를 바탕으로 실제 동작하는 인터랙티브 프로토타입을 제작하여 팀과 논의할 수 있는 수준의 시안을 완성합니다.

■ 클로드 디자인에서 클로드 코드로의 프로젝트 핸드오프
클로드 디자인에서 제작된 시안은 압축 파일로 다운로드하거나 클로드 코드로 직접 명령어를 복사하여 넘길 수 있습니다. 이를 통해 디자인 시스템의 컨텍스트를 유지하면서 실제 개발 코드로 구현하고 수정하는 효율적인 개발 연동 프로세스를 구축할 수 있습니다.

videos.title: Why You’re Bad at Disagreeing (And How to Fix It)
videos.description:
How do you engage in conflict at work without alienating those around you? In this episode of HBR IdeaCast, Harvard Kennedy School professor Julia Minson shares what her research has shown about how we typically disagree with coworkers and direct reports--and how we can do it better. She explains research about why words matter more than intentions, how the goal of changing someone else's mind is often unrealistic, and how to stop disagreements from escalating and upending your culture.

videos.transcript_text: What I always tell people is that a constructive disagreement is a disagreement that leads the two parties to want to talk to each other again. >> Right? So, it's not reaching agreement. It's not building consensus. It's not finding a negotiated compromise. It's can we disagree, but in a way that makes you want to talk to me and makes me want to talk to you at some point in the future. Today we're speaking with Julia Mson of the Harvard Kennedy School. She's the author of the book How to Disagree Better and co-author of the HBR article, A Smarter Way to Disagree. Julia, welcome. >> Thank you. It's great to be here. >> So, why do teams and organizations need to do a better job of disagreeing? >> Well, I mean, disagreement is such a crucial skill for any organization, right? The reason we bring people together into teams is because we want their opinions. If I didn't want another person to express their views, why am I paying for their presence in the room? There's a great quote by William Wrigley Jr. like the Wrigley Field and the, you know, Wrigley chewing gum guy, who said, uh, when two men in business always agree, one of them is unnecessary. Okay. And so, what do teams normally get wrong? Is it they're not disagreeing enough or they're disagreeing in unhealthy ways? >> So, I mean, honestly, I think it's both because it's a system, right? So, when we don't feel like our ideas are going to be received uh with appreciation, with uh receptiveness, we don't want to speak up. And so, you know, we can advise leaders and team members all day long about how disagreement is important, but it's important in these like fairly abstract ways, right? like it'll be good for the company, it'll be good for the team, but the cost to me as an individual if I disagree with my boss or if I disagree with my team member is very immediate and very real. And so people are always making this trade-off between do I want to speak up for the good of the future and have a difficult and unpleasant and risky conversation right now. So there's a real tension there. Yeah, I imagine that um personality differences and cultural differences also come into pretty significant play here also. >> Yeah. So I think you know there's always kind of different factors that predict how well we are at any skill, right? And so disagreement is you know like musical ability, right? Like some people are just better at it than other people, but all of us can get a lot better with a little bit of training and attention to, you know, how we're doing it. Yeah. And so do you encourage the leaders that you work with to embrace disagreement to sort of encourage it among their team members? So what I really work on with leaders is uh a skill set that I call receptiveness to opposing views. >> And it's basically engaging in any disagreement in a way that shows the other person that you're thoughtfully considering their perspective. Because I can tell you that you should disagree with me all day long. >> But if you work for me, you're going to say, "Well, does she really mean it? Am I going to get ostracized? Am I going to get kicked off this project?" Right? So, I have to show with my behavior that I really mean it. And the way I show it is by, you know, showing you that I'm really thinking about what you're bringing to the table and I'm really engaging with it instead of just saying, "Oh, you should disagree." Because disagreement is good for us. >> Yeah. given that you know most of us probably do have a distaste for disagreement particularly in workplace settings and particularly in times that feel divisive and so you don't want to bring that divisiveness to the office you know what's the first step in just sort of overcoming that hurdle as a leader yourself you know even before you start encouraging it on your team how do you sort of get into the mode of okay disagreement is healthy and I actually want it here leaders have a tremendous amount of agency and leverage by modeling the type of behavior that they want to see. Right? So, if I can change my own behavior to demonstrate receptiveness to opposing perspectives, uh then my team members see it. And it's really useful to model the behavior we want to see in very public settings, right? Because if I'm having a one-on-one conversation, then I have shown one person that I'm receptive to their views. If I'm having a regular, you know, team check-in, then every Tuesday I'm showing 10 people that I'm receptive to their views. And so, as I start showing and behaving in the way that I want other people to behave, then I am telegraphing to the world, this is the type of thing that's welcome here and this is the values that we have as an organization. >> Yeah. So I definitely want to dig into sort of how you demonstrate receptiveness to others views and opinions and disagreement. But first let me just ask you there are leaders who say yes I love disagreement but what are the biggest mistakes that they make in modeling disagreement to others? Like what are the problems that you see out there in the world? So I think people who say that they love disagreement they probably do love disagreement but they are not recognizing that they're a minority. Most people don't love disagreement. Um, that's one difference. The other thing is that if you're a leader who loves disagreement, uh, you might be forgetting about sort of the status differences that give people different opportunities to act on the way they prefer to act, right? So, a colleague of mine and I were doing a training in a hospital system a couple months ago, and that hospital system had one of these leaders that loves disagreement. Uh, and then when we got there and we're talking to some of the other employees, you know, fairly senior people, they basically said, "Look, when the executive team disagrees, it sounds like mom and dad fighting, >> right?" And so the people who were in the position of power felt very comfortable with it, but everybody looking on didn't feel nearly as great about it. Right? So that appreciating the fact that other people have different circumstances than you do and different preferences than you do um I think is a really useful thing to do. And what are some other um ways that you think leaders subconsciously suppress disagreement while thinking that they're doing a good job of embracing conflict and embracing viewpoints. So I think a really sort of highlevel, you know, upstream way that we suppress disagreement is by hiring people that uh we agree with, >> right? And it's a it's a very funny thing because of course you should hire people you agree with because those are the smart people because they agree with you, right? You know, maybe they're the smart people, >> right? We right I you know I work at a school of public policy and so a lot of our students manage large public organizations uh and many of them are very like ideologydriven right they sort of went into public service because they have a mission and so they will say things to me like well Julia I work at an environmental nonprofit should I be hiring people who don't care about the environment I'm like yeah you should, right? Because otherwise everybody at your organization is sort of drinking the same Kool-Aid, >> right? >> Um and that I think feels quite counterintuitive to folks. By the time you have a team in place that feels really comfortable, you might have a problem. So your research has identified reasons why most of us are pretty bad at understanding other people's perspectives. So just outline what you found about that. >> Sure. So a lot of my work is grounded in uh an old social psychology theory called naive realism. >> Mhm. >> The idea behind naive realism is that people think that they get it. They like naively believe that their perceptions are a reflection of an objective reality. Right? I see the world as it is. I am a smart, reasonable, good person who basically like I'm with the program, right? And that makes sense because how else could you get through the world? The problem with naive realism is that when we encounter disagreement, we have to say, well, if I'm a smart, reasonable person who basically gets it, why are we disagreeing? >> And the obvious answer to that question is that the other person doesn't get it. >> Right? And because they don't get it, I am going to fix them. >> Okay? >> Right? And of course, fixing then takes different forms. So sometimes you say, "Well, let me tell you how it really is. Let me show you the report. Let me show you the data. Let me give you the customer feedback." And then you will see that I'm right and you're wrong. Right? And that often doesn't fly because of course the other person, they also think that they get it. Uh and they've seen the data and they've interpreted the data in a different way, right? And they have sort of years of experience that dictate their understanding of the situation >> and they prioritize different things. They prioritize different things. Exactly. Exactly. And so, you know, when just sort of telling people facts doesn't work, uh, you jump to, you know, a couple other conclusions that are even more nefarious, which is, you know, one is, well, maybe they're not that smart. Mhm. >> They went to the lesser business school >> and so we can forgive them for not being very good at understanding, you know, complex relationships >> or even worse, they are biased. >> They don't want to get it. You know, if they admit that I am right, it will look bad for them. You know, their budget will get cut or their staff will get cut or they will have to recognize that I'm a better fit for this leadership position. Uh and so they are just sort of intentionally not seeing the light. Yeah. >> Right. And so once you tell that story to yourself inside your head, it's very hard to have a respectful conversation between adults. >> Yeah. And at the same time, we also don't see how they are perceiving us, which is with all those same judgments. Right. >> Exactly. Exactly. Exactly. That's exactly right. So, one of the main points of your book and your article is that to disagree better, you need to focus on not your mindset or your emotions, but on your behaviors. We recently did a podcast with Amar Kisy of Trinity University who talked about the importance of positive intent mindset. Why do you think that narrowing down on the behaviors rather than sort of what you're thinking and feeling ahead of time is most important? Because honestly in like a very practical way I am focusing on ROI. >> Okay. All >> right. So I think that if we all had positive intentions and kind of warmer evaluations of our counterparts and you know had better emotional self-control, the world would be a better place. It's just that's really really hard work. Um and it takes a very long time and there's something that gets in the way which is interpersonal perceptions. Right? So if I think the kindest, nicest, best intention things towards you, there's still two things that have to happen for that to impact our interaction. One is I have to be able to express all that. I have to express it consistently and with signals that you understand, >> right? And then you have to interpret the signal. Mhm. >> And so at every step along that chain, we lose information and we misinterpret each other. Right? So what often happens is I prepare for a conversation that I expect to be difficult by saying, "I'm going to be really patient and I'm going to be curious and I'm going to exercise intellectual humility and I'm going to show empathy, right?" And then I walk into the conversation, the person starts talking >> and like half of my intentions are out the door, right? because I'm still trying but like I am not you know Buddhist monk so I don't have amazing control over my you know emotions I just have like medium decent control right and then I try to show my empathy and I try to show my curiosity but I might accidentally ask a snarky question >> like I didn't intend it to be snarky but it came out to be snarky yeah right and then you are reading all of this and of course this is a disagreement So, you have negative expectations about me, right? And so, the question that I asked that was kind of snarky, that wasn't intended to be snarky, comes across as super snarky to you. Right. >> Right. And so, I'm doing all this work in my brain, but what you're perceiving is not good. >> Yes. >> Right. And so if that's the problem that we're trying to solve, then we need to get sort of like closer in the production chain to the thing that we want, which is the perceiver to experience us as being empathetic and curious and engaged with their perspective. And so that's behavior. >> Yeah. Now this does presume that the goal of the person in the disagreement is to come to a common happy place as opposed to just win the argument. So what do you say to people who are like well no I actually want to win so why should I approach things that way? >> Yeah. Okay. I'm so glad you brought up goals because that's you know it's it's either my second favorite topic or it's tied as being my with my favorite topic. Um the goal of winning an argument. um is generally uh unrealistic, >> right? Uh when you are imagining your winning argument uh and the other person saying, "Oh, I'm sorry, Julia. You were right. I'm wrong. You're so smart." Right? It's never going to happen. My husband's really going to enjoy this conversation. I have to tell you. >> Okay. Go ahead. You know, so because in in any argument again, the math is that both people are living that fantasy, >> right? >> So at best your odds are 50/50, which are not great odds, right? Uh but in reality, most conversations, if a person feels like they're sort of being argued into a corner, they're just going to walk away, >> right? They're going to roll their eyes and they're going to say, "I don't need this." Right. >> Right. And I think that's something we often forget in conversations. It's an optin voluntary activity, >> right? And so if the other person doesn't like how you're treating them, the easiest thing for them to do is to just walk away. >> Yeah. >> Um there are, you know, probably the most familiar example of all of that is teenagers. >> But there are a lot of settings. So for example in healthcare if you're a health care provider and you're trying to persuade a patient to do something they don't want to do get a vaccine or you know take their you know blood pressure medications or get a particular set of tests if they don't want to do it they will leave your office and they will just never show up again >> right and so that's the real risk and so I think we need to be very very careful and thoughtful about what our goals are how realistic they are and what they might lead to inadvertently. Yeah. And in a workplace setting, you know, you might not walk away. You might see whoever has less power in that situation. I mean, you would see a client walk away, right? >> But, um, whoever has less power would perhaps agree with you, and then walk away feeling hugely resentful, maybe talk about you behind your back, say you're a terrible boss, and then eventually leave, which is costly to the organization. >> Right. Exactly. Exactly. >> Okay. So when we talk about behavior change, what exactly do you want people to do? The kinds of behaviors we care about are behaviors that are visible and interpretable, right? So, you know, there's all kinds of, you know, behaviors I could be doing that you don't notice or you can't interpret correctly. >> Uh, and it turns out that the thing that is the most visible and the most interpretable uh in a disagreement is words, >> right? So this is another place where a lot of my research sort of diverges from popular wisdom which is that I think body language is not the thing we should be focusing on >> because body language is very easy to misinterpret >> right um >> or not even notice >> or not even notice right because again we are not trained actors right so our nonverbal signals are really really messy >> um language is also easy to misinterpret but We are far more consistent at interpreting each other's language than we are at interpreting non-verbal behavior. So if we want to clearly communicate engagement with opposing views, we need to use our words. >> Okay. And do we need to get better at both articulating our own views as well as soliciting the opinions of others? >> So I think that's a great question. What tends to happen is that people are very very focused on articulating their own views and they just don't spend enough time soliciting and really engaging with the opinions of others. What I often notice in courses and workshops is that as soon as I ask people to engage with other perspectives, they start playing like amateur therapist. And so then they ask questions and they never express their own views. Mhm. >> They go completely to the opposite extreme which is unrealistic in real life because in real life at some point you need to say what you believe. Right. >> Right. So I think one of the ideas that I really want to get get across to folks is that you can do both. Right. You know you can express your beliefs and you can engage with the ideas of other people and those two things are not uh at odds with each other. You should be able to do both in equal measure. >> Yeah. And so how do you start um training people to pay more attention to their linguistic behavior to what they say? Pay attention to your linguistic behavior, right? Being aware of that uh is step one. And then thinking about what what are you trying to do, right? What are you trying to accomplish? What I always tell people is that a constructive disagreement is a disagreement that leads the two parties to want to talk to each other again. >> Mhm. Right. So, it's not reaching agreement. It's not building consensus. It's not finding a negotiated compromise. It's can we disagree, but in a way that makes you want to talk to me and makes me want to talk to you at some point in the future. >> And so, if that's the goal, >> right? What are the words we use? >> Okay. So, I'd love to walk through just a few roleplay scenarios here so our listeners and viewers just get an idea of what language you're actually talking about. So, say I'm a middle manager who disagrees with my executive level boss on a decision. How should I approach that? So, the first thing I would do, and I suspect it's going to be true for every roleplay you put in front of me, uh, is try to understand the other person's perspective better. Okay? Right? People often jump into persuasion mode. Right? If I explain to them how things really are, then they will recognize the correctness of my view. Yeah. Right? And maybe that's true, but you have no idea where they're coming from and you're just as likely to, you know, frankly make a fool of yourself because you're arguing without insight about the other person's perspective. So, I would start with really exploring the other person's view, which takes time and usually takes more time than we expect it to. Uh but it really sort of protects you from making your own argument with kind of no awareness of the landmines. >> Yeah. So what language specifically would I use again if I'm a subordinate talking to a boss? >> So I would say something like I'm really glad we're having this conversation. I'd like to understand more about your perspective. >> Right? So I don't know what we're talking about in the scenario. Let's say we're talking about a product launch, >> okay? >> Uh and let's say the boss thinks that the product can be launched sooner and I think we need more time. I might say, "Help me understand why it's important to launch it on this particular timeline. We as the team have some concerns about the timeline, but you know, you have been doing this for a long time, and I'd like to hear your vision for how this can get accomplished, >> right? And you try to ask follow-up questions that again show curiosity and show your desire to learn about the other person's perspective because the big risk is that they're going to say something you don't agree with, something you see as unrealistic or something you see as unfair to the team and then you're going to start arguing, right? like you went in, oh, I'm going to, you know, learn and I'm going to understand, but then as soon as the other person says one thing, you start arguing, right? >> Uh, you have to be more patient. >> Okay, that's really hard though. So, if you know my trigger is the boss saying, "Well, why wouldn't you be able to get that done in a week's time >> and they're not respecting my opinion? How do I disagree better with them when they're not disagreeing better with me? Yeah. So, it takes quite a lot of self-control. I I absolutely agree with you there. It takes self-control and it takes time. I think about the goal of modeling receptiveness as sort of a north star. >> And you know, the north star is supposed to be your guiding principle that you don't get distracted from, right? And what often happens in conversation is I go in with that guiding principle and somebody says, "Well, why can't you get it done in a week?" And I get distracted by, you know, that feeling of, "Oh, I'm being disrespected." Or, "Let me tell you why we can't get this done in a week." >> Right. >> Right. Uh, and so you really have to sort of exert some selfmastery to stick to the goal. >> Yeah. >> Right. and say, "Well, you know, I have some concerns, but I would like to hear why it's so important to get this done in a week, right? What is at stake for the team, for you, for the organization? Maybe we can figure something out, but let's let's discuss sort of where we're coming from and what our priorities are." >> Yeah. >> Right. So, don't take the bait, I guess, is what I'm saying. >> Yeah. Yeah. Um, so I suspect that the scripts will all be the same for all other scenarios, but just if you're dealing with a peer or an employee on your team, they should all be handled in the same way. >> Yes. Although here's how status plays into it. In some sense, the boss scenario, you have the least ability to just power your way through, >> right? Because in the end, the boss is still the boss, right? So trying to understand and trying to really make that person feel like you're paying attention to their uh requests uh is a more sure way to get your way >> when you are the lower status person. Right? If you're the higher status person, you can just shove your way through. >> But then the risk is that you're now back to modeling the negative behavior that you don't want to take hold on your team and you have just told the lower status person, >> there's no point disagreeing with me because I won't listen anyway. >> Yeah. Right. >> And then they might treat their colleagues or their subordinates that that way. >> Right. or next time uh they observe something that's potentially catastrophic, they don't bring it to you >> because there was no point, >> right? So, when you're training people to do better at this, what does it look like? You know, do they do role plays? Do they memorize scripts? How does it work? >> Yeah. videos.transcript_text: Right now, every automation you've built in Claude Code dies the second you close your laptop. Scheduled tasks, loops, agents, they all need your machine on. And that's fine if you're just experimenting, but if you'd actually want AI agents doing things [music] while you sleep, like checking your emails, posting updates, monitoring your systems, that's not going to cut it. Anthropic just launched routines in Claude Code, and this is the thing that changes [music] that. But here's the thing, when I first tried migrating my automations over, they didn't just work. There are real gotchas [music] that will waste your time if you don't know them up front. So, in this video, I'm going to show you exactly how to set up routines from scratch, what breaks and why, and give you three automation ideas so you can actually deploy today. So, let's get into number one, what routines are and why it matters. Let me start by making sure that you understand exactly what routines are because there are now three ways to run automations in Claude Code, and if you mix them up, you'll end up frustrated. The first is loop. I did a whole video on this. You can type a prompt and tell Claude to check it on something every 10 minutes, every hour, whatever interval you want. But it lives inside your open session. Close the laptop, kill the session, and the loop is gone. Great for help me right now situations, not for running things while you sleep. The second is scheduled tasks. These are stored automations that survive restarts. Your agents can do things daily, weekly, on a schedule, but they still run on your local machine. Your laptop has to be on and connected. Same problem, just more persistent. And then there's routines. This is the new one. Routines run on Anthropic's cloud infrastructure. Your laptop does not need to be on. You configure it once, you give it a name, you write a prompt that tells it exactly what to do, you connect it a GitHub repo, you set a schedule, and Anthropic's servers handle everything from there. You can literally close your laptop, go to sleep, wake up, and your agent has already done the job. But there's more than just scheduling. There are three ways a routine can trigger. First, a time schedule, hourly, daily, weekdays, whatever cadence you set, minimum once an hour. Second, an API call. Another automation can make a post that fires your routine on demand. That means you can chain automations together or have external tools kick off your agents when something happens. Third, GitHub events. A new pull request, a new issue, a new push to your repo, any of these can trigger the routine automatically. So, this isn't just a cron job, it's a proper serverless trigger system for your AI agent. The reason this matters if you're a creator or an operator is that your agent can now actually work around the clock without babysitting. Posting Slack updates, analyzing analytics, checking your pipeline, monitoring your inbox, all running on Anthropic's infrastructure. You just need to set it up correctly, and that's exactly what I'm going to show you now. Number two, set up your first routine. I want to walk you through every single piece of this because there are more moving parts than it looks like. And if you skip one of them, routines won't work. The first thing you need is a GitHub repository. This is not optional. It's how routines work at a fundamental level. When a routine fires, Anthropic's servers clone your GitHub repo, read your Claude.md, and any scripts or skills you have in it, execute the prompt you gave it, and then when the run is done, that cloned environment gets completely deleted. So, the only files your routine ever has access to are what's in your GitHub repo, not your local machine, just GitHub. Keep that in mind, we'll come back to that in just a second. The second thing, you need a cloud environment. This is a setting profile that configures the Anthropic's side runtime for your routines. Things like your API keys and networking access settings. You can create one from scheduled task panel, give it a name, something like Andy Cloud or production. The most important thing in here is the environment variable section. I'll cover that in detail in the next step because it's where most people's routines break. For network access, start on trusted. If a specific API endpoint gets blocked, switch to full. That's all you need to know. Don't overthink it. Third, write your prompt. This is the actual instruction Claude receives every time the routines fires. Think of it as you're typing a message into Claude Code, but no one is home to course correct if it gets confused. So, the prompt needs to be specific. It has to tell Claude exactly what to do in what order, using what tool. If you have a skill already defined in your Claude.md, you can reference it directly. Run my morning briefing skill. But if you're doing something custom, write out the full order of operations so Claude can execute it without asking questions. Then, set the schedule. Hourly is the minimum, so you can't go tighter than that, and set your permissions. I recommend starting on trusted and only switching if something gets blocked. That's the full setup chain, GitHub repo, cloud environment, prompt schedule, permissions. Every piece has to be there. Step number three, the API key gotcha. Okay, this is the one that got me, and based on everything I've seen people trying this out, it almost gets everyone on the first try. So, pay close attention because this will save you a lot of debugging. When you run Claude Code locally, your API keys live in a .env file on your project folder. Claude knows to look there. Your Claude.md might even reference it. Your API keys are in the .env. That works perfectly on your machine. But here's what happens when a routine fires in the cloud. Anthropic clones your GitHub repo, and your .env is and absolutely should be listed in your .gitignore. You would never push your API keys to GitHub. So, when the cloud environment gets the cloned repo, it has everything from GitHub except the .env. Claude lands in the cloud, tries to find your API key, looks for the .env, finds nothing, and then routines fail. That's it. That's the whole problem. The fix is straightforward, though. Put your API keys in the cloud environment instead of the .env. Go into your cloud environment settings, scroll to the environment variables, and add each key you need. Name them exactly the same as they appear in your local.env, Airtable API key, YouTube API key, whatever it is. Anthropic injects these into the runtime whenever the routines fire, so Claude can actually read them. But there's a second part to this fix. Even with the keys in the cloud environment, Claude might still go looking for the .env just out of habit, especially if your Claude.md mentions it. So, add one explicit line to your prompt, "My API keys are available as environment variables. Do not look for a .env file." That single sentence can save you an entire debugging session. The security rule here, never push your .env to GitHub, not even a private repo. Private repos still have history, and if anyone ever gets access to that repo, they get your keys. Cloud environment variables is the right place for your secrets. Number four, what works and what doesn't. Okay, now I want to make sure that you don't waste your time building a routine around something that's just fundamentally won't work because there's a whole category of automations that will never work in the cloud, and you need to know which ones before you spend an hour on it. The core thing to understand is that every routine is completely stateless. When it fires, it clones your GitHub repo. When it finishes, it deletes the cloned environment entirely. No persistent disk, no cookies from your last session, no local files, no authentication state carried over from run to run. Each run starts from scratch. That means if your automation uses a browser, Playwright, Puppeteer, anything that opens Chrome and relies on saved session cookies, that's not going to work in the cloud. If you set up a browser session locally from a platform that doesn't have an API, and your automation has been working fine because it can read cookies from your last login, that session simply doesn't exist in the cloud runtime. The cloned environment has never logged in anywhere. So, browser-based automation that depend on session state won't transfer over as is. You'd need to switch to an actual API authentication or an API key or OAuth token to make those work remotely. Now, what does persist? Two things. First, if your routine makes changes to your GitHub repo, writes a file, creates a branch, opens a pull request, that gets pushed back to GitHub before the environment is destroyed. So, your output can survive even if the runtime gets deleted. Second, run logs. Every run is stored in your task history. You can go back and read exactly what happens, exactly what errors occurred, what Claude outputs. Use this. This is your debugging tool. The mental model that makes this click. If Claude can reach it through your GitHub repo or through an API call with a key, it will work. If it requires local files, browser sessions, or anything that only exists on your machine, it won't. The good news is that modern platforms have API. And once you move your credential out of the .env and into the cloud environment, most of the existing automations will transfer over with minimal changes. Number five, use cases to set up today. All right, let me give you three specific specific routines that you can set up today. These are designed for creators and operators, not developers, and they all work within the constraints that we just covered. Number one, morning briefing. Every morning at 7:00 a.m. your routine fires. Hit your Airtable, pull your active tasks for today, and sends a Slack message with your top three priorities. You wake up to the briefing in Slack, your laptop is closed, your agent already did the work. This is the easiest one to start with because if you've been using Claude code at all, most of the pieces are already there. You just need to move the credentials to the cloud environment and write a specific prompt. Number two, YouTube comment analysis. Once a week, your routine grabs your last 50 YouTube comments via the YouTube data API, runs an analysis, and pushes a summary file to your GitHub repo. You get a weekly read on what your audience is reacting to without ever manually pulling the data. Just remember the prompt tip from step three. Tell Claude explicitly that the API key is in the environment variables, not in the .env. Number three, pipeline health check. If you've been managing a team or sales pipeline in Airtable, have a routine fire daily. Scan everything in the in progress status, flag anything that hasn't had an update in more than 48 hours, and post an alert to Slack. It's like having a head of ops that checks the pipeline every single day without being asked. Any of these can be set up in under 20 minutes. Pick one that removes most friction from your week and just start there. If you want the exact starter prompts for each of this written out, ready to paste in, they're in our school community. Link is in the description. Free to join. Thank you for being one to stay till the end. Why don't you drop a subscribe and like on this video? I'll see you in next one. Peace.

저희는 이번에 폴더블 폰이 많은 분들의 관심을 좀 받을 거라 생각돼 가지고 이번에 이렇게 최대한 실제랑 비슷하게 제품을 한번 만들어서 보여 드리긴 했는데요. 아 사실 저희가요 지난 영상에서 얼마나 고생해서 이걸 만들었는지 자세히 말씀드리긴 했는데 정말 그 보이지 않은 곳에서 정말 많은 고생고생 개고생을 했습니다. 왜냐면 사실이 정도 수준의 모을 업체 의뢰를 videos.description:
Bonus Day is here… and this is where things get real.

Join Igor Pogany and Dean Graziosi for a powerful live bonus session where they’ll walk you step-by-step through building your very own “AI DNA.”

This is not just theory… this is about giving you a clear, repeatable process you can actually use in your life and business.

If you missed Igor’s Context Sandwich training on Day 1, you can’t afford to miss this. This session builds on that foundation and shows you how to apply it in a way that actually sticks.

Expect a deeper dive, real examples, and a level of clarity that makes AI feel simple, practical, and usable.

If you’re here live, you’re in the right place. Lean in, take notes, and get ready to lock this in.

And if you’re ready to go even further and implement this in your life or business, check out the AI Advantage Bootcamp here 👉 https://aiadvantagesummit.com/aia-bootcamp

Let’s build something real.

AMD 같은 경우는 뭐 GPU도 하고 있잖아요. 많은 걸 하고 있기 때문에 그래서 뭐 주가가 요새 너무 많이 올라서 조금 사기는 부담스럽지만 알아두시면 또 AI 병목이 GPU나 네트워킹뿐만이 아니라 CPU에도 있구나. 요거 혹시 좀 캐치해 두시면 나중에 또 투자 기회를 얻을 수 있지 않을까 생각을 하고 있습니다. 요거는 이제 트렌드 포스에서 재구성을 한 건데 저는 조금 과장돼 있다고 생각을 해요. 자, 에이전틱 AI에서 CPU, GPU 비율 변화라고 돼 있는데 전통 LLM, 전통 채에서는 CPU가 15%를 차지하고 GPU의 부담이 85%였다고 하면요. 요게 이제 1대 1로 권력이 이동합니다. videos.title: 대만 메모리 난야, tsmc 기술 지원에 엔비디아 공급망 포함  | LPDDR SOCAMM 규격 맞출 수 있는 원인 분석 | 삼성, 하이닉스, 마이크론 SOCAMM2 전쟁과 와피지
videos.description:
HBM만 보던 AI 서버 메모리 전쟁에 새로운 전선이 생기고 있습니다. NVIDIA의 차세대 Vera Rubin 플랫폼에서는 GPU 옆 HBM뿐 아니라 CPU 옆 LPDDR/SOCAMM 메모리가 중요해지고 있습니다.
이번 영상에서는 대만 DRAM 업체 Nanya가 NVIDIA 공급망에 들어갈 수 있다는 보도의 의미를 분석했습니다.

이 뉴스는 단순히 작은 메모리 업체 하나가 NVIDIA를 뚫었다는 이야기가 아닙니다. AI 서버에서 전력, 대역폭, 공간, 패키징, 신호 무결성이 모두 메모리 경쟁의 핵심이 되고 있다는 신호입니다. 특히 SOCAMM은 기존 DDR 메모리와 다른 서버용 LPDDR 모듈 구조로, warpage와 접점 안정성 같은 물리적 품질 관리가 중요해지고 있습니다.

TSMC가 Nanya를 도왔다는 보도 역시 DRAM 생산 자체보다는 NVIDIA 플랫폼 검증과 패키징 생태계 관점에서 해석할 필요가 있습니다. 또한 대만 입장에서는 TSMC 중심의 파운드리 생태계에 약한 메모리 고리를 보완하려는 전략적 의미도 있습니다. 

결국 앞으로의 메모리 경쟁은 칩 성능뿐 아니라, 플랫폼 전체를 맞출 수 있는 시스템 경쟁이 될 가능성이 큽니다.

H맨뿐만 아니라 LPDDR 소캠도 그렇고 지금 제가 정말 안 좋게 봤던 CXL조차도 인텔이 주도를 하고 또 메모리 계층이 다양화되면서 티어링이 된다라는 새로운 측면에 오면서 드디어 CXL을 한번 좀 이렇게 상용화해 볼 수 있지 않을까 이런 기대감이 스멀스멀 다시 올라오겠어요. 상황이 이렇게 많이 바뀌고 있다는 거죠. 그러니까 성능이나 전력, 공급막 같은 것들을 결정하는 모든 것들이 메모리 중심적으로 가고 있다는 겁니다. 그 GPU만 있어도 메모리가 부족하면은 AI 서버가 못 나가니까. 물론이 모든 것들은 또 에너지가 없으면은 못 나가게 될 겁니다. 그래서 최근에는 막 우리나라 현대중공 같은 배를 만드는 곳에서이 발전기 용어로 만드는 엔진을 가져와 가지고 데이터 붙인다. 이런 얘기도 나오고 있죠. 그래서 대만 입장에서 대만이라는 국가 입장에서 생각해 봅시다. 그러면은 TSMC와 뭐 서버 ODM들도 있겠지만도 네트워킹 쪽은 원래 대만이 좀 잘하거든요. 근데 메모리가 약하니까이 정도를 밀어 주면은 대마 자체적으로 자립할 수 있는 뭔가를 만들 수가 있잖아요. 그런 쪽에서 요런 것들을 서로서로 도와주는 것이 아닐까 이런 생각이 들고 그런 입장에서 낫냐라는 기업들이 사실 이번에 매출을 많이 올랐을 때 메모리 상강급은 아니지만 대만 내부에서 거의 유일하게 키울 수 있는 카드가 될 텐데 TSMC가 좀 이렇게 직접 디랩을 만드는 건 아니더라도 패키징 쪽이라든가 워핏 쪽 관리를 하는 방법이라든가 이런 노하우들 돈을 받고서라도 지도를 해 줄 수 있고 그러면서 엔비디아는 이런 구조야 이런 것들 잘 신경 써 봐 이렇게 서포팅만 해 주더라도 훨씬 더이 개발 기간이라든가 기술 격차를 빠르게 다갈 수도 있겠죠. 그래서 디램을 만든게 아니라 TSMC 중심으로 이렇게 플랫폼의 어떤 검증 형식을 맞춰갈 수 있는 것들이 TSMC가 워낙 경험이 많고 업게 리더기 때문에 그런 부분들은 난에게 전수해 줄 수 있지 않을까? 물론 이거는 공식 발표가 아닙니다, 여러분. 다 이거 소설이에요. 소설일 수도 있고 아닐 수도 있는데 기사에서 나온 내용들을 좀 살펴보면은 어 그 정도로도 할 수가 있겠는데라고 싶은 거죠. 난 같은 기업들이 메모리가 불안일 때 풀 수가 없죠. 근데 메모리 같이 이렇게 쇼티질일 때 빨리 치고 나가야 되는데 중국은 그나마 미국이 제재를 해서 빨리 못 자라고 있는데 남녀 같은 기업은 그래도 조금조 가고 있으니까 훨씬 더 똘똘하게 만든 그런 소행 같은 것들 물량 많이 넣을 수 있는 것들을 넣어 가지고 확실히 매출을 발생시켜서 성장을 할 수가 있겠죠. 더군다나 또 덴스남 같은 경우에는 공급망을 메모를 상관한테만 기대는 것이 아니라 당연히 공급망을 더 확장을 하려고 하겠죠. 지금 다양한 부분들이 공급망을 다변화하면 할수록 싸게 후러칠 수 있으니까 그런 것들을 계속 역할을 할 건데 지금은 워낙 디램이 쇼티지니까 그런 역할을 못 하고 있지만도 미리미리 준비를 한다라고 볼 수도 있겠죠. 물론 난가 모든 거를 다 커버를 할 수 없을 거고 뭔가 세컨 소스라든가 뭐 특정한 라인업에 대해서만 지원할 수도 있습니다. 요건 이제 사실이 아니니까 앞으로 어떻게 될지는 지켜봐야 될 거고 다만 앞으로 이렇게 계속 생산을 하면서 메모리 규모를 키워 가는 우리나라도 그랬잖아요. 옛날에 그 엄청난 인텔이 메모리 사업부를 다 가지고 있을 때 그리고 일본의 기업들이 메모리를 평정하고 있을 때 이럴 때를 생각해 보면은 그때부터 삼성이나 현대 하이닉스 시저부터 그때부터 꾸준히 이렇게 만들어 와 가지고 우리나라 기업이 지금 세계 1위가 된 거지 않습니까? 그 똑같은 시나리오처럼 아주 오래 걸리는 시간이 될 수가 있다 하더라도 벌써부터 움직임이 있을 수 있다라는 거. 그럴수록 삼성이나 하이닉스는 넥스트를 위해서 더 준비를 해야겠죠. 그래서 난 소식을 정리해 보면서 우리나라의 메모리 업체들의 앞으로의 방향성에 대해서 한번 같이 생각해 보는 시간 가져보았습니다. 지금까지 에로였습니다.

videos.title: NVIDIA Nemotron은 그냥 AI 모델이 아니네요... Nemotron DevDay Seoul | 네모트론이 보여준 AI의 진짜 방향, 모델보다 중요한 데이터와 학습 구조
videos.description:
NVIDIA Nemotron Developer Day Seoul 현장에 다녀왔습니다. 이번 영상에서는 Nemotron이 단순한 모델이 아니라 어떤 방식으로 만들어지고 활용되는지를 설명했는데요. AI 모델 개선을 위해 단순히 가짜 데이터 생성이 아닌, 합성 데이터가 왜 중요한지, 그리고 단순 생성이 아니라 검증과 반복 구조가 핵심이라는 점을 다룹니다.
실제 행사장에서는 Nemotron이 에이전트 형태로 확장되는 구조와 OpenClaw 같은 시스템과의 연결에 관하여 시연도 진행하였는데요. 지난 3월 GTC 2026에서 매우 핫했던 시연 현장을 한국에서 최초로 경험해보는 시간이었습니다.
또한 왜 AI가 한국을 제대로 이해하지 못하는지, 데이터 분포 관점에서 풀어보는 내용도 있었는데요. Nemotron-Personas-Korea 사례를 통해 로컬 데이터의 중요성도 살펴봅니다.
결국 NVIDIA가 보여주려 한 것은 모델 하나가 아니라 AI를 만드는 전체 공정이라 볼 수 있는데요.
앞으로 AI 산업이 모델 경쟁을 넘어 어떤 방향으로 움직일지 이해하는 데 초점을 맞췄습니다.
